name: DeepAR: Probabilistic Forecasting with Autoregressive Recurrent Networks
key_paper: Salinas et al., 'DeepAR: Probabilistic Forecasting with Autoregressive Recurrent Networks', International Journal of Forecasting, Vol. 36(3), 2020 (arXiv:1704.04110, first posted 2017; journal publication 2020)
algorithm_description: DeepAR is a probabilistic forecasting model that learns a global autoregressive recurrent model across many related time series simultaneously. At each timestep t, an LSTM encodes the history of the time series (plus covariates) into a hidden state; that hidden state is then mapped to the parameters of a chosen likelihood distribution (e.g., Gaussian, Negative Binomial, Student-t) from which the next observation is sampled. During training, teacher forcing is used: the true past values are fed as inputs, and the loss is the negative log-likelihood of the observed next value under the predicted distribution. During inference, the model autoregressively samples from the predicted distribution at each step, feeding the sampled value back as input to produce full sample paths (Monte Carlo trajectories) over the forecast horizon. These sample paths are then aggregated to obtain quantile estimates or predictive intervals. The key innovation is learning a shared model across all series in the dataset, enabling knowledge transfer from data-rich series to data-poor ones and producing calibrated uncertainty estimates rather than point forecasts.
action_space_handling: DeepAR is a forecasting architecture, not an RL policy, so it does not represent a discrete action space in the RL sense. The 'action' at each step is the emission of a distribution parameter vector (e.g., mean mu and standard deviation sigma for Gaussian, or alpha and beta for Negative Binomial). The model conditions on the previously sampled (or observed) value and the current hidden LSTM state to produce these parameters. Because the output is a continuous distribution rather than a discrete set, there is no combinatorial action space to manage — all uncertainty is captured in the predictive distribution. Adapting DeepAR to lottery (a discrete combinatorial output) would require replacing the likelihood head with a multi-label Bernoulli or Categorical distribution, which is a significant architectural departure from standard DeepAR.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: Standard DeepAR does not produce combinatorial outputs (sets of k distinct numbers from {1..N}). It produces a scalar or vector probabilistic forecast at each horizon step. To generate a lottery play, one would need to adapt DeepAR to output a probability vector of length N (pool size), then sample k numbers without replacement using the predicted probabilities as weights — this post-hoc sampling approach does not enforce inter-number correlations during training. An alternative adaptation is to use an autoregressive Bernoulli head (predict P(number_i is drawn) for each i conditioned on previous selections), but this is not native to DeepAR and would require significant custom engineering. The standard DeepAR output is a predictive distribution over the next scalar value, not a set.
sequential_generation_strategy: DeepAR uses a recurrent autoregressive generation strategy over the time dimension: each forecast step is conditioned on all previously generated (sampled) values in the forecast horizon. This temporal autoregression means the model captures dependencies across draws over time (draw t depends on draw t-1, t-2, etc.) but does NOT natively model intra-draw correlations (which of the 7 numbers within a single draw co-occur). The generation is sequential along the time axis, not sequential within a single draw. To model within-draw structure, a separate multi-label output head would be needed, making DeepAR a partial solution: it handles temporal dynamics well but not intra-draw combinatorial structure.
gradient_estimator_type: DeepAR uses maximum likelihood estimation with standard backpropagation through time (BPTT) via the LSTM. Because the output is a parametric distribution and the loss is the negative log-likelihood of the observed continuous value, there is no discrete sampling in the gradient path during training (teacher forcing is used, so true past values feed into the LSTM, not samples). No REINFORCE, Gumbel-softmax, or straight-through estimator is needed. This makes DeepAR training highly stable and low-variance compared to RL-based methods. The gradient estimator is simply standard BPTT — exact and unbiased for the chosen likelihood family.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: DeepAR does not natively enforce combinatorial constraints (selecting exactly k distinct numbers from {1..N}). Its output is a parametric univariate or multivariate distribution, not a discrete set. Post-hoc constraint enforcement (e.g., sampling without replacement from predicted probabilities, or applying a top-k filter) must be added externally if DeepAR is used as a lottery play generator. This is a fundamental architectural mismatch: the model architecture does not reason about distinctness, cardinality constraints, or set membership during training. Any constraint enforcement is a post-processing step and cannot guarantee that the predicted distribution captures the true combinatorial structure of lottery draws.
sample_efficiency_rating: medium-low — DeepAR's key strength is learning a shared model across many related time series, which dramatically improves sample efficiency when the dataset contains hundreds or thousands of series with thousands of timesteps each (the original M4/electricity dataset regime). In the lottery-nn context with only 3 lotteries and ~100 draws each (300 total data points across all series), DeepAR's cross-series transfer learning advantage essentially disappears — there are too few series and too few timesteps to learn meaningful global patterns. The LSTM requires enough historical context (SEQUENCE_LEN steps) to warm up its hidden state, further reducing the effective training data. Empirically, Amazon's internal DeepAR deployments typically involve thousands of product demand series; sub-200-sample single-series regimes are outside its validated operating range.
regularization_built_in: DeepAR includes several implicit and explicit regularization mechanisms: (1) LSTM dropout (applied between layers and to recurrent connections) — standard and configurable; (2) Likelihood-based loss acts as regularization through the distributional assumption (e.g., Gaussian likelihood penalizes overconfident predictions via the sigma term); (3) Global model training across multiple series acts as a form of multi-task regularization — the shared LSTM weights cannot overfit to any single series in isolation; (4) Lagging and scaling: DeepAR applies per-series scaling (dividing by the series mean) before training, which improves numerical stability and acts as a form of data normalization. On a dataset of only 3 series with 100 draws each, the multi-task regularization is weak, making explicit dropout and early stopping essential.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: 1) Insufficient warm-up: LSTM hidden states require multiple past timesteps to encode meaningful context; with only 100 draws total and a window of 20, the effective number of non-overlapping training windows is ~5 per lottery — severely limiting gradient signal. 2) Distributional misspecification: if the chosen likelihood family (Gaussian) does not match the true data distribution (which for lottery numbers is discrete uniform within a fixed pool), the model produces poorly calibrated uncertainty estimates regardless of the sample size. 3) Over-reliance on covariates: DeepAR heavily leverages time-varying covariates (day of week, holiday flags, etc.) for demand forecasting; lottery draws have no meaningful calendar covariates, stripping away one of DeepAR's strongest inductive biases. 4) Mode averaging: with sparse data and a Gaussian likelihood, DeepAR tends to predict the mean of observed values rather than the multi-modal structure of lottery numbers. 5) Hidden state memorization: with very few training trajectories, the LSTM can memorize specific historical sequences rather than learning generalizable temporal patterns.
data_regime_evidence: The original DeepAR paper (Salinas et al. 2020) validates on: M4 Competition dataset (100,000 series, 18-2048 observations each), electricity demand dataset (370 series, 26,304 hourly observations each), parts demand dataset (1,046 series, 51 weeks each), and traffic dataset (963 series, 17,544 hourly observations each). The minimum series length tested is approximately 51 observations (parts demand). The minimum number of series tested is ~370. No experiment uses fewer than 100 total data points, and no experiment uses a single time series or fewer than 3 series. The claim of small-data suitability comes from the multi-series transfer learning property, not from demonstrated performance on isolated short series. [uncertain: minimum_training_samples_tested for single-series regime] There is no published evidence of DeepAR performance degradation curves at sub-200 total observations across all series combined. Third-party benchmarks (Makridakis M5 Competition 2020, Monash Time Series Repository 2021) do not test DeepAR in the lottery-sized data regime.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: [uncertain] No finite-sample convergence guarantees exist for DeepAR. As an LSTM trained via MLE with BPTT, convergence theory reduces to standard non-convex optimization for RNNs, for which only asymptotic results (infinite data) are available. The distributional output adds a well-defined probabilistic loss (negative log-likelihood is proper and strictly convex in the distribution parameters for exponential family likelihoods), but the LSTM parameterization is non-convex. Empirically, DeepAR is known to require many series and long histories to converge to well-calibrated uncertainty estimates; with fewer than 10 training series, convergence to meaningful distributions is not empirically established.
reward_distribution_handling: DeepAR is designed specifically to handle skewed, non-Gaussian reward/value distributions by outputting a full parametric predictive distribution rather than a point estimate. It supports multiple likelihood families: Gaussian, Student-t (heavy tails), Negative Binomial (count data with overdispersion), and Beta (bounded data). For lottery prediction, the sparse reward structure (~95% zero-hit plays) is a fundamental mismatch: DeepAR treats the time series values as real-valued observations to forecast, not as sparse reward signals from plays. The 'forecasting' task — predicting which numbers will appear in the next draw — does not map cleanly to the reward-modeling task of Actor-Critic play generation. Adapting DeepAR to model the reward distribution over plays (rather than the number distribution over draws) would require a non-standard extension. Minimum draws for stable distributional estimation is empirically around 50-100 observations per series in published results.
credit_assignment_granularity: DeepAR operates at the level of forecasting individual draw outcomes (which numbers appear), not at the level of assigning credit to individual plays or number selections within a play. There is no credit assignment mechanism in the RL sense — DeepAR does not have a policy that receives rewards; it has a likelihood model that predicts future observations. If adapted as a play scoring model (estimating the probability of each number appearing), it provides number-level scoring that could be used to derive play-level credit, but this is not native credit assignment — it is a prediction step that must be coupled with an external RL or scoring mechanism.
diversity_mechanism: DeepAR generates diverse predictions naturally via Monte Carlo sampling: multiple sample paths are drawn from the predicted distribution at inference time, each producing a different forecast trajectory. For lottery play generation, this translates to sampling multiple independent plays from the predicted number probabilities — however, this is the same as temperature-softmax sampling and does not model inter-number correlations. True play diversity (generating distinct, non-overlapping sets) requires either: (a) post-hoc deduplication of sampled plays, (b) diversity-promoting sampling (DPP, or explicitly conditioning each new play on previously generated ones), or (c) a non-DeepAR mechanism. DeepAR itself does not provide any diversity mechanism beyond the stochasticity of its predictive distribution.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: DeepAR is fully compatible with offline training from a fixed historical dataset — this is its primary design mode. It trains on historical draw sequences without any environment interaction. At inference time, it generates probabilistic forecasts using only the historical context, with no requirement for new data. This makes it operationally compatible with the lottery-nn use case (one draw per week). However, DeepAR is a forecasting model, not an RL policy, so 'offline RL compatibility' is a category mismatch: DeepAR does not learn from rewards or optimize a policy. It would need to be used as a component within an RL pipeline (e.g., as a world model or as a number-probability predictor feeding into an Actor-Critic), not as a standalone offline RL algorithm.
key_dependencies: PyTorch (core); GluonTS (Amazon's official time series library, provides DeepAR estimator, data loaders, and evaluation metrics — pip install gluonts); MXNet (original DeepAR implementation; now deprecated in favor of PyTorch Lightning backend via gluonts[torch]); PyTorch Lightning (optional, used by GluonTS PyTorch backend); pandas, numpy (standard). For a custom PyTorch-only implementation: no additional dependencies beyond PyTorch itself.
estimated_lines_of_code: 200-350 lines for a custom PyTorch DeepAR adapter — LSTM encoder (reusing SharedLotteryTransformer's embedding layer, ~50 lines), likelihood head (Gaussian or Negative Binomial parameter output, ~40 lines), training loop with teacher forcing (~80 lines), Monte Carlo inference sampler (~60 lines), integration adapter mapping DeepAR number-probability output to play generation format (~80 lines). Alternatively, 50-100 lines using GluonTS PyTorch backend with standard configuration.
transfer_learning_compatibility: Partial compatibility — the SharedLotteryTransformer encoder produces sequence embeddings that could initialize the context vector for a DeepAR-style LSTM decoder, but the architectures are structurally different (Transformer vs. LSTM). The transformer backbone can serve as a feature extractor whose output feeds into a small DeepAR-style LSTM forecasting head, but the LSTM hidden state must still be initialized (typically from zero) and trained from scratch. Full weight transfer is not possible between a transformer encoder and an LSTM. A more compatible approach would be to add a probabilistic output head (Gaussian NLL loss, uncertainty estimation) directly to the existing SharedLotteryTransformer without introducing an LSTM at all — this would be 'DeepAR-inspired' rather than true DeepAR and would offer better transfer learning compatibility.
specific_application_in_project: In lottery-nn, DeepAR would serve as a probabilistic number-frequency predictor: given the last 20 draws as input context, output a calibrated probability distribution over each of the 50 possible numbers (for LottoMax) appearing in the next draw. This replaces the current deterministic softmax output of the SharedLotteryTransformer with a full predictive distribution (e.g., Gaussian or Bernoulli likelihood per number). Concretely: (1) add a Gaussian NLL or Bernoulli BCE-with-uncertainty head to the SharedLotteryTransformer; (2) at inference time, sample multiple number-probability vectors from the predictive distribution (Monte Carlo dropout or explicit distribution sampling); (3) use these sampled probability vectors to generate candidate plays via weighted sampling without replacement; (4) the spread across samples provides uncertainty-aware play generation. This applies to all three lotteries via the existing per-lottery heads in model_swarm.py. Key limitation: DeepAR's multi-series transfer advantage is irrelevant with only 3 lotteries and 100 draws each — a simpler MC Dropout uncertainty head on the existing transformer would achieve comparable results with far less complexity. Recommended for Phase 3 only, after Actor-Critic and simpler probabilistic heads are validated.
replaces_or_extends: Extends the existing SharedLotteryTransformer per-lottery output heads — adds a probabilistic likelihood head (distributional output) alongside or replacing the existing BCEWithLogitsLoss head, enabling uncertainty-aware play generation without replacing the transformer backbone
existing_open_source_implementations: 1) GluonTS (Amazon, official): github.com/awslabs/gluonts — DeepAREstimator available in both MXNet (legacy) and PyTorch backends; pip install gluonts[torch]; most complete and production-tested implementation; 2) pts (Probabilistic Time Series): github.com/zalandoresearch/pytorch-ts — clean PyTorch-native DeepAR implementation; 3) DeepAR PyTorch reimplementation: github.com/jingw2/demand_forecast — lightweight standalone PyTorch DeepAR; 4) Darts library: github.com/unit8co/darts — includes DeepAR via its RNNModel with likelihood support; pip install darts; 5) Nixtla's neuralforecast: github.com/Nixtla/neuralforecast — DeepAR included alongside N-BEATS, N-HiTS; pip install neuralforecast. GluonTS[torch] is the recommended starting point.
benchmark_results: Salinas et al. 2020 (IJF): DeepAR achieves state-of-the-art ND (normalized deviation) and rho-50/rho-90 quantile losses on Electricity (ND=0.054, vs. ARIMA 0.154), Traffic, Parts, and M4 Competition datasets. Outperforms Prophet, ETS, ARIMA, and DeepState on 7 of 8 tested datasets. M4 Competition 2018: DeepAR-based entries achieve top-5 results on monthly and quarterly series but underperform on weekly/daily series where pattern complexity exceeds data density. Makridakis M5 Competition 2020: DeepAR variants place competitively but are outperformed by LightGBM and ensemble methods on the M5's 42,840-series dataset, suggesting that for large structured datasets tree-based methods remain competitive. Monash Time Series Forecasting Repository (Godahewa et al. 2021) benchmark: DeepAR ranks 3rd-5th on most univariate series but shows performance degradation on series shorter than 100 observations. No published benchmark directly evaluates DeepAR on lottery draw prediction or similar combinatorial discrete tasks.
notable_use_cases: 1) Amazon product demand forecasting (primary domain): millions of product-level demand series with thousands of observations each — the regime for which DeepAR was designed and where it excels; 2) Energy load forecasting: electricity consumption prediction with clear periodicity and multiple related series — GluonTS tutorials use electricity as primary benchmark; 3) Retail inventory optimization: Salinas et al.'s own application — predicting intermittent demand (sparse, with many zero observations), which has some structural similarity to lottery's sparse hit distribution; 4) Financial time series (experimental): stock price prediction with uncertainty bands — limited success due to non-stationarity; 5) Healthcare: patient vital sign prediction with uncertainty — similar short-series, high-noise regime to lottery draws. None of these use cases involve combinatorial discrete set generation, which is the critical gap for lottery-nn application.
